Chapter 44

The seed, and why the data tells a story

Uniform random data makes every screen look the same and every one of them look wrong. This generates an incident.

By the end of this chapter

Produce demo data where every view has something to show, identically on every machine.

None of the interesting behaviour in this product is reachable from random input: the percentile that moves, the flame graph with one fat bar, the alert that pends and then fires. A generator that emits noise produces a latency chart that is flat noise and a trace where every span is the same length.

A normal afternoon, and twenty minutes that are not

Traces are generated as trees rather than as independent spans, because the viewer’s whole job is to reassemble a tree — and data that was never a tree would let a broken assembler pass every test you thought to write. Every four seconds of the six hours, a few requests arrive at the gateway, which calls checkout, which calls payments and inventory; inside the incident window more than half of the payment calls take seconds instead of milliseconds, and the spans above them carry the error.

The latency is log-normal-ish rather than uniform, because real latency is never symmetric: mostly fast, with a tail. A uniform generator produces a p50 and a p99 that are close together, which is the one thing latency never is.

Seeded, so the demo is the same demo

A fixed seed matters more than it sounds: a screenshot in the documentation stays true, and an end-to-end test can assert on a specific trace. It is also what lets the seed plant one deliberately incomplete trace at a known id, which turns the orphan-handling path from a coin toss into something a test can name.

And why it runs under plain Node

The seed imports schema.ts, keys.ts and auth.options.ts — and deliberately not db/index.ts or auth.ts, which read $app/env/*. Those modules are generated by SvelteKit’s Vite plugin and do not exist outside it, so importing them would mean booting a Vite dev server to insert some rows. The header above says so; the cost is that the seed reads its own environment.

Node reads .env for it: the db:seed script is node --env-file-if-exists=.env scripts/seed.ts. The file used to be loaded by a process.loadEnvFile('.env') written above the import lines, as though it ran first, and it did not. import declarations are hoisted — every imported module is evaluated before the first line of the module that imports it — so the call ran after all of them, and the seed worked only because none of them happens to read process.env as it loads. A flag on the command puts the order where it looks.

And .env is optional, not assumed, which is what -if-exists says. prepare-e2e-db.js and a CI job put the variables straight into the environment and have no file to load, and a variable that is already set wins over the file. The very first version of the line, a bare process.loadEnvFile('.env'), made the end-to-end database refuse to seed on any machine without one.

The split is between environment and configuration

The seed duplicates the *environment* — three lines reading process.env — and shares the *configuration*, which is one function in auth.options.ts. The alternative, configuring Better Auth a second time, works until the day the two disagree about the password minimum, at which point the seed produces an account the application rejects and the error says nothing about why.

Two more things the first version got wrong

SQLite has a hard limit on bound parameters in one statement, and a thousand rows of twelve columns is comfortably past it. The error is too many SQL variables, which is a much less obvious message than it should be.

And the ids are seeded from a counter rather than from a timestamp. The first version used the span’s start time, which is unique most of the time — two requests in the same four-second tick can land on the same millisecond, and then their ids are identical and the insert dies on the unique index. That is also why they are OpenTelemetry-sized: 32 hex characters for a trace and 16 for a span. Shortening them to 8 for readability made the collision likely enough to hit at sixteen thousand spans.

Checkpoint

  • pnpm db:seed twice produces the same traces, ids and incident, placed relative to when it ran.
  • Every view — table, chart, flame graph, waterfall, alerts — has something to show.
  • There is an incident in the data, and an alert that fires because of it.
